title: Input, Process, Output
intro: The basic breakdown of any computation!

title: Input, Process, and Output
paragraphs: Most programs can be broken into three main parts: input, process, and output.
Input is information that enters the program, process is what the program does with that information, and output is the result produced.
This is called the Input-Process-Output (IPO) Model.

title: Planning with IPO Charts
paragraphs: An IPO Chart identifies what information a program needs, what it will do with that information, and what result it will produce.
IPO charts help organize a program before any code is written.
Each section describes the purpose of that stage rather than the exact Python syntax.

title: Input - User Input
paragraphs: Input is information provided to a program so it can perform a task.
Programs can receive input from many sources, including keyboards, sensors, cameras, and files.
In Python, input() is used to collect text entered by the user in the terminal.
The program waits at input() until the user types a response and presses Enter.
expectedOutput: What is your name? Mr. Forsyth
initialOutput: What is your name? Mr. Forsyth

title: Input - Input Prompts
paragraphs: The string inside input() is called the prompt.
It is displayed before Python waits for the user's response.
A clear prompt tells the user exactly what information they should enter.

title: Input - Storing User Input
paragraphs: The value returned by input() can be assigned to a variable.
This allows the program to remember the user's response and use it later.
The variable stores whatever text the user entered.
code:
name = input("What is your name? ")

print(name)
expectedOutput:
What is your name? Mr. Forsyth
Mr. Forsyth
initialOutput:
What is your name? Mr. Forsyth
Mr. Forsyth

title: Process – Using Input in Your Program
paragraphs: A process is an action performed on data, such as a calculation, modification, or decision.
After receiving input, a program can process that information and then display a result.
The example code in this slide includes some concepts covered later in these slides.
code:
number = input("Enter a number: ")

number = int(number)
doubled = number * 2

print(f"Double your number is {doubled}.")
expectedOutput:
Enter a number: 5
Double your number is 10.

title: Process - User Input Is a String
paragraphs: The input() function always returns a string, even when the user types a number.
This means "5" and 5 are different values: "5" is text, while 5 is an integer.
If Python tries to use the string "5" in a mathematical operation, it can cause an error because it is not being treated as a number.
initialOutput:
Enter a number: 5
TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str

title: Process - Casting Input to int or float
paragraphs: Casting converts a value from one datatype to another.
int() converts a string into a whole number.
float() converts a string into a decimal number.
This allows numeric user input to be used in calculations.
code:
whole_number = input("Enter a whole number: ")
whole_number = int(whole_number)
print(whole_number)

decimal_number = input("Enter a decimal number: ")
decimal_number = float(decimal_number)
print(decimal_number * 2)
expectedOutput:
Enter a whole number: 5
5
Enter a decimal number: 2.5
5.0
initialOutput:
Enter a whole number: 5
5
Enter a decimal number: 2.5
5.0

title: Output with print()
paragraphs: Output is information produced by a program.
In Python, print() is commonly used to display output in the terminal.
It can display strings, variables, numbers, and other values.

title: Output - Combining Strings with Concatenation
paragraphs: Concatenation means joining strings together using +.
Because concatenation joins strings, other datatypes must first be converted using str().
This works well for simple messages, but larger statements can become difficult to read.
code:
name = "Alex"
score = 10

print("Player: " + name + " Score: " + str(score))

title: Output - Combining Output with Commas
paragraphs: Multiple values can be placed inside print() by separating them with commas.
Python automatically adds a space between the values and can display different datatypes together.
This is a simple way to combine text and variables.
The downside to using commas is that it always adds a space between your values.

title: Output - Formatted Strings
paragraphs: A formatted string, or f-string, allows variables and expressions to be inserted directly into a string.
Add f before the opening quotation mark and place values inside curly brackets {}.
F-strings are usually the clearest way to create output containing several variables.
They can also include numbers without converting them to strings first.

title: Formatting Text - Escape Characters
paragraphs: An escape character changes how Python interprets the character that follows it.
Python uses the backslash \ as its escape character.
(Make sure you don’t get confused with the forward slash character / which is not an escape character).
This allows special characters, such as quotation marks, to be placed inside strings without ending the string early.
Notice that the escaped quotation marks change to orange!

title: Formatting Text - The Newline Character \n
paragraphs: \n creates a new line inside a string.
It can be used in normal strings, formatted strings, or input prompts.
This is useful when output needs to be split across multiple lines.

title: Pro Tip: Using \n in an Input Prompt
paragraphs: A newline can also be placed inside the prompt used by input().
This moves the user's typing position onto the next line.
It can make longer prompts easier to read.
expectedOutput:
Enter your name:
Mr. Forsyth
Hello, Mr. Forsyth!
initialOutput:
Enter your name:
Mr. Forsyth
Hello, Mr. Forsyth!

title: IPO Wrap Up
paragraphs: Python programs commonly follow the Input-Process-Output (IPO) model.
input() collects information from the user and always returns that information as a string, so numeric input may need to be cast with int() or float().
print() displays output, and values can be combined using commas, concatenation, or f-strings, with f-strings usually providing the clearest formatting.
Escape sequences such as \n and \" can also be used to control how strings are displayed.
